POPULATION: Karaganda (Karagandy) is a major city in central Kazakhstan and capital of the Karaganda Region, with a population of 497,777 at the 2020 Census, up from 459,778 in 2009 and 436,864 in 1999 [W]. Later figures vary: 518,263 in 2023 [44], an estimated 514,741 in 2025 [45], and 505,941 for the urban area [43]. Sources disagree on its rank: the fifth-most populous city in Kazakhstan [W] versus the fourth largest [47]. It lies about 230 km southeast of the capital, Astana [W], within a three-hour drive of it [76]. The name comes from caragana bushes, which are abundant in the area [W].

FOUNDING (COAL DISCOVERY AND THE OLD TOWN): The city traces its origin to 1833, when a local shepherd, Appak Baizhanov, allegedly found coal on the site [W][1][25]. Source [1] calls him a shepherd boy [1]. The attribution is contested: there are several points of view on who first discovered Karaganda coal [3]. A 1932 article in a republican newspaper made Baizhanov the recognized discoverer of the basin [2]. In 1856 the merchant Ushakov bought the land, on today's Maikuduk territory, from two Argyn (Kazakh tribe) families for 250-255 rubles [5]. Ushakov could not stay afloat for long and sold the business to the Russian merchant Ryazanov [9]. Sources differ on when the first mine opened: one says the first mines opened by 1856 [8], while another says the first working, the Ivanovskiy pit, was not built until 1857, on the spot now occupied by Mine No. 18 [7]. Early artisanal coal mining supplied the Spassky Copper Smelter, and the first workers' settlements appeared [24]. From 1857 to 1887 the mines produced a total of 302,800 tons of coal [22]. In 1886 the mines employed 200 Kazakhs and 10 Russian workers [23]. Accounts of foreign involvement vary in timing. One says foreign entrepreneurs controlled development from the 1860s [10]. Another says Russian merchants, workers from nearby villages and French and English entrepreneurs were drawn in by the late 19th century [W]. A third places Russian merchants and then British and French entrepreneurs in the early twentieth century [12]. The mines were later abandoned, and the site is still labeled the "Old Town" on city maps, though almost nothing remains there [W].

SOVIET CITY AND FORCED LABOR: In the late 1920s Soviet geologists examined the deposits, and authorities set up the Karaganda Coal Trust [W]. Planners intended a dozen mines and drafted a city for an estimated 40,000 workers [W]. Mining resumed in 1930 in temporary structures, but supplies were inadequate, living conditions were poor, and 1930 output fell below expectations [W]. In February 1931 a railroad connection brought in supplies and highly qualified personnel [W][26]. Construction of a city designed to support the mines and serve as an industrial junction began in 1931 [15]. Karaganda became a village in 1931 and was declared a city in 1934 [W]. Planner Alexander Ivanovich Kuznetsov laid out master plans from 1934 to 1938 [W]. The Karlag prison camp network was created to supply slave labor for the mines [21][W]. Sources disagree on its start date: established by the NKVD later in 1931 [W], on December 19, 1931 [19], or opened in 1930 and operating until 1959 [31]. Karlag held approximately 65,000 prisoners and forcibly resettled people [30]. During the Stalinist purges, Germans, Karachais, Kalmyks, Chechens, Ingush, Greeks and Crimean Tatars were sent there [W]. The 1939 population is given as about 100,000, roughly half of them prisoners [W], or as 166,000, swelled by forced labor [28]. Settlers dug their own dugouts in the steppe, then built damp, unheated adobe barracks [48][49]. Two to three families shared a single dugout [54]. Stoves were fueled with weeds and dried dung gathered in the steppe [55]. Deportees traded clothing for dung fuel [56], and one mother bartered sewing and knitting for milk and potatoes [57]. Special settlers had to report to the commandant's office every ten days [50]. Cold, scurvy, lack of bread and water and rampant typhus caused mass deaths in 1931–1933 [52]. In the 1940s up to 70% of inhabitants were ethnic Germans, mostly Volga Germans deported on Stalin's order in 1941 [W]. Solzhenitsyn's camp in One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich was near Karaganda, and Flora Leipman wrote of Karlag in The Long Journey Home [W]. Robert F. Kennedy and Justice William O. Douglas were refused visas to visit the city four times [W].

ECONOMIC ENGINE: Coal mining has been the city's central industry and remains a key sector [W]. Today the city is an industrial hub for coal mining and metallurgy [42]. On 2 April 1942 the basin's miners shipped a trainload of coal to Moscow [4]. By 1978 Karaganda's miners had produced one billion tons of coal [32]. The basin had as many as 26 mines in Soviet times and 8 as of 2023 [W][73]. Methane in the mines is a major safety hazard [41]. On 28 October 2023 a fire at the Kostenko mine, run by ArcelorMittal Temirtau, killed at least 32 people [W][74]. In December 2024 ArcelorMittal completed the sale of its Kazakh assets to Qazaqstan Investment Corporation [36]. In June 2025 the successor company Qarmet announced a $3.5 billion five-year plan, with $300 million for mine safety [39]. Local water is insufficient for the city, so the Irtysh–Karaganda Canal was built in the 1960s to bring Irtysh River water more than 400 km [W].

GROWTH AND DECLINE: Kuznetsov's plan for 300,000 residents was exceeded by the late 1960s, a new plan targeted 600,000, and that figure was passed by the 1980s [W]. After the USSR collapsed, the economy fell sharply and mass migration followed [33]. Many mines closed, leaving miners with fewer opportunities [34]. The population fell 14% from 1989 to 1999, and over 100,000 people have since emigrated to Germany [W]. The city was once Kazakhstan's second-largest after Almaty [W]. It was briefly considered for the capital in the early 1990s but lost to Astana [W].

SURPRISES AND VIVID DETAILS: On 22 October 1962, Soviet Test 184, a 300-kiloton nuclear burst 290 km above Zhezkazgan, induced currents in a 1,000 km buried power cable and set the Karaganda power plant on fire [W]. This was the most severe electromagnetic pulse effect ever observed [W]. Across the former USSR, the exchange "Where?" — "In Karaganda!" became a punchline about the middle of nowhere [W]. A monument to that catchphrase was created on 28 May 2011 [W]. The Fedorov Reservoir, built in 1941, is a flooded coal mine pit [W][69]. Aleksei Stakhanov directed Mine No. 31 from 1943 to 1957 [W]. The Miners' Glory monument was erected in 1974 [35]. FC Shakhter Karagandy beat Celtic 2–0 in 2013 Champions League qualifying [W]. The city has the 150-hectare Central Park, built 1935–1941 [W]. It is also home to the Miners' Palace of Culture and the Fatima cathedral, opened in 2012 [W]. IQAir ranked it highest in Kazakhstan for PM2.5 in 2017–2022 and 23rd in the world [W]. The record low is given as −42.9 °C in 1938 [W] or −42.8 °C in December 1938 [62]. The average January temperature is about −13.5 °C [60].

FOUNDING: Spanish Lookout is a Mennonite settlement in the Cayo District of Belize in Central America [W]. It was settled in 1958 by Kleine Gemeinde Mennonites from Mexico [W][1][12]. One source says approximately 75 families came from the Quellen Colony, Chihuahua [1], while another says the founders came from the colony of Los Jagueyes, Chihuahua, Mexico [20]. The Kleine Gemeinde were of Dutch-Russian background, had settled in Canada in the 1870s, and immigrated to Mexico in 1948 [4]. The first group landed in March 1958 [5]. Sources give several reasons for leaving Mexico. They objected to a new social welfare law in Mexico, and arable land was more readily available in Belize [W]. Early settler Gerhard Koop said Mexico did not want to sell much land to the Mennonites and they needed more land [8]. Mexico could no longer promise that their children would be exempt from the draft [11]. They faced discrimination and persecution in Mexico [12]. Several delegations were sent to investigate the land and opportunities in Belize [10][17]. The group purchased land from Miss Olga Burns [17], described as former timber tracts [18]. The Government of British Honduras granted the Mennonites the right to run their own churches and schools with their own teachers [13]. In return, the Mennonites agreed among other things to bring in capital investment of 500k British Honduras dollars [14]. They also had to pay all the costs of establishment [29]. One reason George Price invited the Mennonites was to lessen Belize's economic dependence on neighbouring countries [15]. On January 16, 1963, it was decided to keep the name Mennonite Community Spanish Lookout [19].

EARLY HARDSHIP AND MIGRATIONS: The area was jungle when the settlers arrived, bisected by only a few rutted logging trails [3][6]. A tree served for a while as a church building [5]. Frustration led several people to move back to Mexico after the first year [30]. Over time, some families left for Manitoba and Nova Scotia, Canada [W]. In 1966, over 30 conservative families left for Paraguay over conflicting beliefs about modernization [W]. Another group left and started a colony in Lower Barton Creek [W]. Natural growth nonetheless maintained, and then increased, the population [W][28]. In the 1980s, refugees from Guatemala and El Salvador arrived for employment and for schooling for their children [W][34].

POPULATION: The population was 1,108 in 1987 [W][26] and 1,786 in 2000 [W][27]. It was 2,300 in 2005 [W]. In 2010 it was 2,253 people in 482 households [W]. The 2022 census counted 3,108 [W]. Other sources give over 3,000 [22], 2,900 [24], and around 1,600 [25]. In 2010, the population was 86.8% Mennonite and 8.7% Mestizo, with small Mixed, Caucasian, Ketchi Maya and Creole shares [W]. Residents speak Plautdietsch as their mother tongue, and most also speak English and Spanish [W]. In 2010, 87.9% spoke English, 87.2% German and 27.3% Spanish [W].

ECONOMIC ENGINE: The settlement covers 18,500 acres (7,500 hectares) on the north side of the Belize River [2]. It is largely agricultural, with some light industry, furniture making, prefabricated wood houses and the only oil field in production in Belize [W][37]. Vegetables were the main income for the first 10 years but were no longer produced in sizable quantity by the late 1980s [31]. In 1986, products included eggs, broiler hens, beans, corn, grain sorghum, milk, cheese and beef cattle [32]. Today it is a major exporter of beans, corn, chicken and dairy products [W]. Sixteen farmers and businessmen formed Western Dairies in 1967 [33]. Western Dairies is the country's only commercial milk producer [W][35]. Its large Spanish Lookout restaurant gets very busy on weekends with customers from all over the country [W]. Visitors often stop there to see ice cream being made [62]. Quality Poultry Products is the largest chicken producer in the country and runs the Chicken Express restaurant chain [W]. Country Foods is Belize's largest egg supplier [W]. Koop Sheet Metal is the largest roofing supplier and has been a major supplier since Hurricane Hattie [W]. Caribbean Tire/Caribbean Motors is the largest vehicle and tire vendor in Belize, with a branch even in Chetumal, Mexico [W]. The town was the country's leader in tire hardware and steel imports [38]. Farmer's Trading Center is the country's second biggest combined hardware and grocery retailer [59]. Farmer's Trading Center, Quality Poultry Products and Western Dairies are owned by the community [60]. Farmers Light Plant Corporation is the largest power provider not connected to the national grid [W]. About 30% of its power comes from solar, and the rest from crude oil and other methods [W]. One study credits community cohesion, agriculture and entrepreneurship for the settlement's economic growth [36].

OIL: Spanish Lookout has had Belize's only commercial oilfield since at least 2006 [W][39][71]. At its peak, the field produced an average of 5,000 barrels per day and is now in decline [40]. Belize Natural Energy extracted roughly 4,130 barrels per day in 2010, falling to approximately 986.92 barrels per day later [41]. An official cited an economic limit of about 235 barrels, expected to be reached around 2030 [42].

SURPRISES AND DETAILS: The community is quite modern, using cars and other modern conveniences [W]. Its overall impression is more like rural North America than Central America [W][67]. Visitors see tidy farmhouses, white-fenced fields, paved roads, and showrooms for cars and tractors [68]. One account describes semi-trucks, motocross, huge tractors, new Chevys and GMCs, and air-conditioned buildings [69]. Old Order and traditional Mennonites from Springfield, Red Bank and Pine Hill charter vehicles to come to Spanish Lookout [70]. The settlement is reached via the George Price Highway, mainly over the Iguana Creek Bridge [W]. The Central Farm entrance crosses the river on a hand-cranked ferry that carries vehicles [W][57]. Sources call this ferry one of Belize's two hand-cranked ferries [W][57], while another source calls it the 3rd hand-cranked ferry in Belize [56]. The river crossed is named as the Belize River [W] or the Macal River [54]. At the crossing the river is about 150 feet wide, and the crossing takes 8 to 10 minutes of cranking [46][54]. The Mennonites built the ferry, and it was once the only access route [44]. It was originally sited at Mennonite Beach, where the settlers arrived in 1958 [45]. The ferry has a rush hour of non-Mennonite employees and customers [47]. It closes during heavy rains [48] and operates in daylight only [49]. Passengers walk on while the driver positions the car [50]. Vendors on the ferry sell hot corn and watermelon [51][52]. Most businesses close at noon for an hour so all employees can have lunch [61]. At the Spanish Lookout Expo, no alcohol is sold and there is no raucous music [63]. Traditionally, women did laundry on Monday (one woman starts at 3 a.m.), baked on Friday, and cleaned on Saturday ahead of Sunday [64][65].

raw_research: Ghadames is an oasis town in the Nalut District of the Tripolitania region in northwestern Libya, about 462 km (287 mi) southwest of Tripoli and near the borders with Algeria and Tunisia [W]. Atlas Obscura puts it 'a tad less than 300 miles' from Tripoli [82]. It is known as 'the pearl of the desert' [W][17]. It lies in the pre-Sahara between the Great Erg sand sea and the Al Hamada el-Hamra stone plateau, and it is built around the Ain al-Faras spring [1]. WATER AS THE REASON TO SETTLE: Ghadames has a hot desert climate, with July average highs around 41°C (105.8°F) and only 73.1 mm of rain a year [W]. Its position at a water source in the middle of the desert made it an important or ideal place to settle [W][7]. One study calls the freshwater spring Aïn al Faras 'the only source of life' [68]. A legend recorded by Archnet tells of a man who rode back to a spot where his horse dug in the ground and unearthed a spring, which became the main source of water for much of Ghadames' history [3]. The spring's French tourist-guide name translates as 'Source of the Mare' [69]. FOUNDING AND EARLY HISTORY (sources conflict on dates): Wikipedia says archaeological evidence suggests settlement since the 4th millennium BC [W]. Archnet cites Paleolithic and Neolithic occupation [15]. Other sources give about 3000 BC [17][18] or 'at least 5000 years' [16]. Two travel sites instead say the 4th century BC [19] or around 300 BC [20]. UNESCO says indigenous peoples called the Phazanii occupied it from at least the late first millennium BCE [9]. One source says the oasis was originally inhabited by the Garamantes [10], while others say Berber communities first lived there, relying on its wells [6][11]. The first written records are Roman, when the place was called Cydamus [W][10][21]. The Roman proconsul Lucius Cornelius Balbus invaded it under Augustus [W][22]. Wikipedia dates that invasion to the 1st century BC [W], and other sources specify 19 BC [21][22][23]. A permanent Roman garrison was established under Septimius Severus [W][24][26]. One source specifies Severus's reign as AD 193-211 and says Ghadames became a garrison town for the Third Legion [27]. The emperor may have visited around AD 202 [W]. The Romans withdrew a few decades later during the Crisis of the Third Century [W]. By the 6th century the population had been converted to Christianity by Byzantine missionaries, and a bishop lived in the oasis [W]. Muslim Arabs ruled it from the late 7th century, and the population quickly converted to Islam [W]. One source says Muslim Arabs developed its present compact structure in the 7th century [32]. Others say the present old town is probably about 800 years old and is the third town in the area, with the town centre having moved around the oasis [28][29][30]. NAME (disputed) [14]: Wikipedia and Temehu derive it from the Berber tribe name Tidamensi, which became Roman Cydamus and then Ghadames [W][13]. Archnet reports a popular Arabic etymology, 'yesterday's lunch' [4]. Temehu explicitly rejects that etymology [12]. ECONOMIC ENGINE, HISTORICAL: From Arab rule until the 19th century, Ghadames was a base for the trans-Saharan trade [W]. Historical texts call that trade the town's essential activity [33]. It sat at a junction of caravan routes [8]. It linked an east-west route from Egypt to Mauritania with a north-south route from the Mediterranean to Kano [40]. Caravans from the south brought slaves, gold, leather and hides, ostrich feathers, ivory and incense [35]. Return caravans carried cotton goods, cloth, sugar and European manufactured products [36]. Ghadames was an important town in the trans-Saharan slave trade [W]. Its traders were found as far away as Timbuktu [34], where Ghadames always had settlers representing it [W]. Tripoli merchants advanced European goods to Ghadamis traders on credit [38]. Close cooperation with the Tuareg, particularly the Adjer Tuareg, was key to the traders' success [39]. The trade mainly benefited nobles, who also owned gardens, herds and slaves [37]. The town declined as the trans-Saharan trade disappeared [43]. In the mid-19th century the French explorer Henri Duveyrier wrote of the beginning of trade's decline after abolition, though the source text is cut off at 'abolition of slave...' [44]. ECONOMIC ENGINE, TODAY: The oasis survives on farming and tourism [45][77]. The compact housing left much of the land free for palm gardens and orchards [42]. Camels still thrive even though the caravans have stopped [51]. One source says locals often trade dates with commercial convoys crossing the Sahara [76]. Tourism collapsed after the post-2011 instability, as foreigners no longer felt safe [46][49]. A local festival seeks to attract visitors, and organisers hope for Algerian tourists if a nearby border crossing reopens [47][48]. The festival features feasting, dancing, music, and horse and camel races [50], along with traditional dress, weddings and rites of passage for young men [79]. POPULATION (conflicting): About 10,000, mainly Berbers [W][45]. CityFacts gives 8,782 [53]. The Libya Observer gives 25,000 [54]. SURPRISING FEATURES AND DETAILS: Houses divide functions vertically [W][62]. The ground floor stores supplies, the family lives on the first floor above covered alleys that form an almost underground network of passageways, and open-air rooftop terraces are reserved for women [W][62]. The rooftops are often interconnected so women can use them as a thoroughfare [63]. The old town is built of mud and almost completely covered except for small ventilation holes [64]. Another source describes it as made of mud, lime and palm trunks [82]. The design keeps the town cool in summer and warm in winter [65]. Interiors have geometric wall paintings, rugs, and wall-hung copper pots and mirrors that refract light [66]. The town gates close every day at sunset and open at sunrise [75]. The walled old town was divided among seven clans, each with its own district and festival square [W]. Water from the spring was allocated to each garden by a pierced cup, the gâddous, which served as the unit of minimum irrigation time [69]. The water flowed through five canals whose flows were proportioned 1:3:9:27:81 [70][71]. It was distributed to the seven tribal sectors on a strict time basis [72]. The channels total about 13 km and have caretakers [73]. They run along the centre of the lanes or along the tops of walls [78]. The community still manages the system [74]. ABANDONMENT AND RETURN: The government built new houses outside the old town in the 1970s [W][59]. Sources differ on when people left the old town. Wikipedia says it was de-populated through the 1990s [W]. Other sources say families began leaving in 1981 [52] or were moved out between 1984 and 1986 [60]. Tours Libya says only one family refused to abandon its quarters [58]. No one lives there permanently [56][57], but many residents return in summer because the old architecture beats the heat [W][55][56]. UNESCO inscribed the old town in 1986 [W][17]. It was on the World Heritage in Danger list from 2016 to 2025 because of civil-war damage [W][47], and it was removed in July 2025 [61]. Moustapha Akkad filmed interior scenes of Medina for 'The Message' there [W]. Other modern history: Italy occupied the town in 1911 [W]. It was the capital of the French Military Territory of Fezzan-Ghadames from 1943 until 1951 [W]. NTC forces entered on 30 August 2011 [W]. After the Libyan National Army captured the town, the entire Tuareg community was forced to flee [W].

raw_research: Grise Fiord is an Inuit hamlet on the southern tip of Ellesmere Island in the Qikiqtaaluk Region of Nunavut, Canada [W]. Its Inuktitut name, Aujuittuq, means 'place that never thaws' [W]. The name Grise Fiord means 'pig inlet' in Norwegian; Otto Sverdrup of Norway named the fiord during an expedition around 1900 because he thought the walruses there sounded like pigs [W]. POPULATION: The 2021 census counted 144 residents, up 11.6% from 129 in 2016 [W][66][68]. Those residents lived in 58 of 64 private dwellings on a land area of 332.9 km2, a density of 0.4 per km2 [W][67]. Other sources give different figures: the Government of Nunavut lists a population of 160 [69], and an Irish Times piece refers to the hamlet's 132 inhabitants [70]. Grise Fiord is the largest community, and the only public community, on Ellesmere Island, and Canada's northernmost public or civilian community [W]. It was incorporated as a hamlet in 1987 [68]. FOUNDING: The Canadian government created Grise Fiord, along with Resolute, in 1953 through a forced relocation of Inuit families from Inukjuak, Quebec [W][1]. Inukjuak was then called Port Harrison [1][29]. Sources disagree on how many families came. Wikipedia says eight families were relocated [W]. The Qikiqtani Truth Commission says six Inuit families arrived at Craig Harbour on August 29, 1953, with their qimmiit (dogs) and possessions, accompanied by RCMP Constable G. K. Sargent [6]. It adds that two more families arrived the following month [7]. Another source says three families were relocated [29]. Across both destinations, 19 Inuit families from Inukjuak were moved to Resolute Bay and Grise Fiord in the 1950s [2]. More than 90 Inuit were moved roughly 2,000 kilometres in 1953 and 1955 [19]. The first warning that families would be separated came aboard the ship C. D. Howe, when they were already in High Arctic waters [8]. The families were promised homes and game to hunt, but they found no buildings and very little familiar wildlife [W]. The area was purported to be plentiful in game, although no wildlife studies had been done there and no Inuit had permanently lived there [16]. They were promised plentiful caribou [36]. Instead they were told they could catch only one caribou per year per family [37]. Accounts of the promised return differ. Wikipedia says they were told they could go home after 'two or three years' if they wished, and that the offer was later withdrawn because it would have damaged Canada's sovereignty claims [W]. The Truth Commission quotes Henry Larsen, Officer Commanding the RCMP's 'G' Division, promising that families would be brought home at the end of one year [26]. Although officials called the relocatees 'volunteers' [27], evidence shows the families most dependent on government assistance were more likely to be relocated [28]. WHY: The motive is disputed. Many sources say the relocation was done partly or wholly to assert Canadian sovereignty in the High Arctic during the Cold War [W][19][21][22]. At the time, the United States and the Soviet Union were scaling up Arctic activity [20]. The Truth Commission says sovereignty reinforced the project in the minds of some key players [23]. The government's position is that the relocation was humanitarian [18]. Its stated purpose was to move Inuit from 'overpopulated, depressed areas' where they depended on relief payments [17]. One writer notes that the 2010 apology reiterated the official position that the move had nothing to do with sovereignty [25]. The Hickling Report concluded the government had done little wrong beyond accidents [24]. Background to the move: in 1922 Canada set up RCMP detachments on Ellesmere Island to assert its claim [13]. These detachments were meant to act as small 'colonies' demonstrating Canadian influence [14]. Craig Harbour, the RCMP detachment, lies about 55 km east of Grise Fiord [30]. The families were soon moved to the Lindstrom Peninsula, about 70 km west of the detachment [9]. In 1956 the RCMP moved its post closer to the Lindstrom settlement, establishing a detachment at Grise Fiord [11]. When a school was built in 1962, the Lindstrom Inuit moved there too [12]. The Truth Commission dates the school and housing to 1961 [46]. The settlers survived by learning beluga migration routes, eventually hunting over 18,000 km2 each year [W]. AFTERMATH: In 1993 the government held hearings on the relocation [W]. The Royal Commission on Aboriginal Peoples' report recommended a settlement, and the government paid CAD 10 million to survivors and their families [W]. A formal apology followed in 2010 [W][2]. A monument by local artist Looty Pijamini shows a woman with a boy and a husky gazing toward Resolute Bay [W]. It faces a companion statue by Simeonie Amagoalik in Resolute, which shows a lone man looking back toward Grise Fiord, symbolizing separated families [W]. Minister John Duncan unveiled the Grise Fiord monument on September 10, 2010 [W]. ECONOMY: The economy is described as subsistence-based [W][50]. Hunting remains central, with quotas covering seals, walruses, narwhal, beluga, polar bears and muskox [W]. Ringed seals are available year-round and are the primary hunting focus [32]. The region has been called a superior sealing area [31]. Walrus was considered the best dog food [33]. Polar bear pelts came to make up 55% of a family's cash income by the late 1960s [38]. A polar bear quota of 27 per year was set in 1967 and had risen to 32 by 1973 [42][44]. The muskox quota was 12 in 1969 and was raised to 20 in 1973 [43]. Today many workers are employed by Inuit organizations and by the territorial or municipal government [51]. Guiding and outfitting, including sports hunting, is an important income source [W][52]. Outfitters can earn good money [58]. Carving, traditional clothing and other crafts also bring in income [W][53]. Muskox hides and horns provide local income [55]. There is no mining or other major industry [54]. One resident, Terry Noah, sells beluga jerky and smoked polar bear meat to the community [60]. Ecotourism is developing [W], and cruise ships enter the fiord in summer [94]. Avalanche and rockfall risk leaves no room for the town to expand [W]. SUPPLY AND ACCESS: No roads connect to the hamlet [W]. Its link to the outside world is a 1,675 ft (511 m) airstrip with one of the most difficult approaches, cautioned for very experienced pilots only [W][81]. In the 1970s the territorial government seriously considered shutting the community down because planes struggled to get in [82]. Only one sealift arrives each year [W][71]. In late August 2025, that sealift carried 70 tonnes of goods to the co-op [72]. A tanker brings oil and aviation fuel meant to last 12 months [70]. Grise Fiord has Nunavut's third-highest grocery prices [74]. The mayor cited $50 pickles, $50 ketchup and $27.99 coconut [75]. A February 2025 video showed jam at $35 and pickles at $66 [77]. SURPRISES AND DETAILS: The average yearly temperature is −16.5 °C [W]. Temperatures rise above 0 °C for only four months a year and can drop below −50 °C [93]. The settlement lies 1,160 km north of the Arctic Circle [W]. Polar night runs from about early November [87]. Even then, a faint orange glow is visible to the south at noon [90]. The sun does not set from April 22 to August 20 [91]. In winter, travel is limited to the town site and a patch of land to the east called Nuvuk [W]. Houses are wooden and built on platforms because of the permafrost [W][101]. There is no central plumbing [102]. In 1970 Bell Canada set up what was then the world's most northerly telephone exchange [W]. Kids attend Umimmak School, Canada's northernmost school [97]. A 1992 study found Grise Fiord had the lowest crime rate of the communities examined [W]. Comedian Billy Connolly camped alone on the nearby pack ice for a 1995 BBC documentary [W]. Notable people from Grise Fiord include P.J. Akeeagok, Nunavut's 6th premier [W].

FOUNDING: Freetown is the capital and largest city of Sierra Leone, a major Atlantic port city in the Western Area. [W] Before Europeans arrived, local Temne and Loko people lived in villages near the future city site. [W] The earliest known group in the estuary area was the Bullom people, and Mane invaders established chiefdoms there in the 1540s and 1550s. [W] In January 1568 the English slave raider John Hawkins helped the Mane king Flansire destroy Bonga, a town of around 10,000 people in the area that would become Freetown. [W] Before Freetown existed, Portuguese slave traders used slave steps carved from stone near the Naval Wharf to move enslaved Africans to ships. [W] The abolitionist Granville Sharp selected the site in 1787 as a haven. [1] That year a 'Province of Freedom' was formed through the combined initiative of London's 'Black Poor' and Sharp. [2][W] The Committee for the Relief of the Black Poor, set up by Jonas Hanway and Granville Sharp, organised the 1787 settlement. [W] Sources differ on its size: Wikipedia says 400 formerly enslaved people came from London. [W] Another source says that of 411 who embarked, 377 went ashore. [7] A third source says 96 passengers died between Plymouth and Sierra Leone. [8] The settlers founded Granville Town, named after Sharp, on land obtained from Koya Temne subchief King Tom, with regent Naimbana also involved in the purchase. [W][9] Some historians question whether the Koya leaders understood the agreement as permanent, since they had a different conception of property. [W] Disputes followed, and King Tom's successor King Jimmy burned the settlement in 1789. [W][11] Alexander Falconbridge came in 1791 to relocate the surviving Black Poor settlers, who re-established Granville Town near Fourah Bay, in today's Cline Town. [W][12] The chartered trading Sierra Leone Company took responsibility for the settlement in 1791. [13] Sources name its founders differently: one says Granville Sharp, Thomas Clarkson, Henry Thornton and John Clarkson formed it. [14] Another says William Wilberforce organized it. [26] Its first chairman was the banker Henry Thornton, whose outlook was less utopian than Sharp's. [15] In 1791 Thomas Peters, an African American veteran of the Black Pioneers, went to London to report the grievances of Black people in Nova Scotia. [W][18] There he learned of the Sierra Leone Company's plans. [W][18] Black Loyalists in Nova Scotia were tired of harsh weather and racial discrimination, and land grants there had been slow. [W][17] The Company promised the Black Loyalists full rights as British subjects and upward of 30 acres of land. [19] Lieutenant John Clarkson, RN, an abolitionist, was sent to Nova Scotia to register emigrants. [W] On January 15, 1792, 1,196 women, men and children sailed from Halifax harbour. [22] Other sources give the number as about 1,200, or more than 1,100, or an estimated 1,196. [20][W][24] Peters recruited roughly a third of them. [24] They sailed in 15 ships and reached St. George Bay between 26 February and 9 March 1792. [W] Sixty-four died en route, and Clarkson himself fell ill. [W] Wikipedia dates the founding to March 11, 1792, by 1,196 African Americans under Clarkson at the foot of the Cotton Tree. [W][23] The women stayed on the ships while the men cleared jungle until they reached a large cotton tree. [W] Then everyone marched to the tree as their preachers sang "Awake and Sing of Moses and the Lamb." [W] Nathaniel Gilbert preached a sermon under the tree. [W] Reverend David George of South Carolina held the first recorded Baptist service in Africa. [W] The land was christened 'Free Town' by order of the Company directors. [W] Clarkson became the first governor. [W] Settlers built Freetown on an American grid pattern, with Water Street the widest road. [W] Although Freetown's bicentennial was celebrated in 1987, it was formally founded in 1792. [W] One historian argues that without the Nova Scotians it is hard to see how the colony could have survived. [25]

EARLY HARDSHIP: The settlers arrived at the very end of the dry season, leaving little time to build shelter. [56] Clarkson wrote that "nothing made of Steel can be preserved from Rust." [58] Supplies from England rotted in the heat. [59] In early April 1792 the settlers were put on half rations. [60] They waited a long time for farm lots, and the first forty lots measured five acres. [63] Most settlers relied on food from the company store. [64] In 1793 settlers petitioned against currency redeemable only at the company store, against Governor Dawes's favouritism, and against receiving less land than Clarkson had promised. [W] Some men fished with home-made boats and hunted antelope and wild boar. [65] Settlers planted pumpkins, beans and cabbage from Nova Scotian seeds. [66] They adopted local rice, cassava, millet and kola nut as staples. [67] The French pillaged Freetown in 1794, and the settlers rebuilt it. [W] By 1798 it had 300 to 400 houses with stone foundations and wooden superstructures. [W][68] These houses became the model for the Creole 'bod oses.' [W][70] In the words of one source, "Owning property [such as a Krio home] was a mark of freedom." [71] In 1800 the Nova Scotians rebelled and were suppressed with the help of about 550 newly arrived Jamaican Maroons. [W][27] The Maroons received the rebels' land and gained their own district, Maroon Town. [W]

WHY IT GREW: Freetown became a Crown Colony in 1808. [W] From 1808 to 1874 it was the capital of British West Africa. [W] It was also the base of the Royal Navy squadron enforcing the ban on the slave trade, which landed liberated Africans in Freetown. [W] Sources conflict on how many: more than 50,000 'recaptives' between 1807 and 1864 according to one, some 70,000 between 1808 and 1864 according to another. [43][44] Liberated Africans passed through the stone King's Yard Gate, inscribed "any slave who passes through this gate is declared a free man." [W] The recaptives were the largest group forming the Creole people. [W] Creoles prospered as traders and entered the professions. [36] Some recaptive traders bought auctioned cargoes of captured slave-trade goods and sold them inland. [38] Freetown has long been a center of trade. [39] The hinterland was declared a protectorate to prevent the French from cutting off trade in kola nut, plasas and pepper. [41] Freetown served as a naval base in both World Wars and was the assembly point for SL convoys to Britain in World War II. [W]

ECONOMIC ENGINE: The economy revolves around the harbour on the Sierra Leone River estuary. [W] Wikipedia describes it as one of the world's largest natural deep-water harbours and the largest natural harbour in Africa. [W] Queen Elizabeth II Quay receives oceangoing ships and handles the country's main exports. [W] The city is the country's commercial, financial and transportation centre and hosts most national corporate headquarters and international companies. [W][45] Industries include food and beverage processing, fish packing, rice milling, petroleum refining, diamond cutting, and the manufacture of cigarettes, paint, textiles and beer. [W] Britannica also lists confectionery among the city's industries. [45] Another source says Freetown's economy revolves around trade, mining and agriculture. [46] Informal work dominates. [49][50][51] In the Western Area more than 60% of the labour force works informally. [49] In transport, the second-highest generator of jobs, 85% of jobs are informal. [50] One study puts informal workers at 91% of all Freetown workers. [51] Informal settlements make up 36% of settlements. [48] Over 68 areas have been identified as slums. [82] Coastal residents hesitate to leave flood-prone communities because of sociocultural and livelihood ties. [83]

POPULATION: The 2024 census put Freetown's population at 1,347,559. [W] Other estimates conflict with this and with each other. [28][31][32][33] They include approximately 1 million (12% of the national population), a 2026 metro estimate of 1,429,000, a 2025 urban estimate of 1,935,761, and a 2026 estimate of 474,425. [28][31][32][33] No ethnic group forms more than 27% of the population. [W] Temne people are the largest group. [W] Krio is the dominant language and is spoken as a first language by over 20% of residents. [W] Muslims are the majority, and Muslims and Christians live side by side peacefully. [W]

SURPRISES AND VIVID DETAILS: The Cotton Tree marks the city's christening. [W] Fourah Bay College, founded in 1827, is the oldest university in West Africa. [W] Its first student, Samuel Ajayi Crowther, became the first indigenous Bishop of West Africa. [W] The international airport is at Lungi, about 17 km away across the estuary. [W] Travellers cross by ferry, hovercraft, water taxi, banana boat or helicopter. [W] At low tide, operators wade into the sea and hoist passengers and luggage above the water. [W] At the end of Ramadan, the Lantan Festival sees clubs haul lanterns up to twenty feet long and ten feet high through the streets on wheeled iron chassis, lit by generator-powered bulbs. [W] The 'Paddle' masquerade wears a costume of leather, sequins and sea shells. [W] Streets hum with the honking of poda-podas (minibuses) and kekes (auto-rickshaws). [81] An earlier observer described fishermen lying in dug-out canoes with a fishing line on each big toe. [75] In 2021 Freetown appointed its first heat officer, Eugenia Kargbo. [W] On 14 August 2017 a mudslide on Mount Sugar Loaf killed over 300 people in Regent. [W] Mayor Yvonne Aki-Sawyerr was sworn in in 2018 and re-elected in 2022. [W]

FOUNDING: Vostok Station is a Russian research station in inland Princess Elizabeth Land, Antarctica, founded by the Soviet Union [W][3][4]. It was established on 16 December 1957, during the International Geophysical Year, by the 2nd Soviet Antarctic Expedition [W][1][4][21]. One source conflicts on the year, stating the station was established in 1958 during the International Geophysical Year [14]. The site was chosen for its position near the South Geomagnetic Pole, the point where the Earth's magnetic dipole axis crosses the Earth's surface [1][8][9]. The location was expected to be favorable for studying the ionosphere and the effects of magnetic storms [10]. In mid-1996 the South Geomagnetic Pole was approximately 100 km from Vostok [15]. The station's name means 'east' and comes from the Vostok, the lead ship of the First Russian Antarctic Expedition, captained by Fabian von Bellingshausen [W]. Another source describes the Vostok as a sailing sloop of the Antarctic expedition of 1819–1821 [13]. Since 1957 Vostok has been a year-round research base of the Complex Antarctic Expedition, which was renamed the Soviet Antarctic Expedition in 1959 [5][6]. The station was temporarily closed from January 1962 to January 1963, from February to November 1994, and during the winter of 2003 [W].

LOCATION: The station sits at 3,488 m above sea level [W][1][4]. It is around 1,300 km from the Geographic South Pole, in the middle of the East Antarctic Ice Sheet [W][3]. It is also near the southern pole of inaccessibility [W]. It is one of the most isolated established research stations in Antarctica [W]. The AARI gives its distance from Mirny Station as 1,410 km [40]. Wikipedia says it was supplied from Mirny on the coast [W].

POPULATION: Wikipedia says the station normally hosts 30 scientists and engineers in summer and 15 in winter [W]. Other sources say about 30 in summer and about half that in winter [34]. Another gives around 30–35 researchers each summer, which in Antarctica means December, January and early February [33]. The new complex is designed for up to 35 people in summer and 15 in winter [19][32]. One report on the new wintering complex's trial operation says six expedition members and three dozen technicians would remain for the winter [39]. Winterers include scientists in meteorology, aerology, geophysics, magnetology and oceanography, plus support staff [29].

ECONOMIC ENGINE: The only activity is scientific research, with no commercial activity [31]. Research includes ice core drilling and magnetometry, along with actinometry, geophysics, medicine and climatology [W]. The first ice drilling at Vostok took place in 1958 [12][22]. In the 1970s Soviet drillers took cores 500–952 m deep [W]. Later holes reached 2,202 m in 1984 (Hole 3G), 2,546 m in 1990 (Hole 4G) and 2,755 m in 1993 (Hole 5G) [W]. Drilling stopped at 3,623 m in 1996 at the request of the Scientific Committee on Antarctic Research, over fears of contaminating Lake Vostok [W]. That core, drilled with the French, produced a record of past environmental conditions stretching back 420,000 years and covering four previous glacial periods [W]. One source says that, short on funds as the Soviet Union collapsed, the Russians shared the cores with French scientists for analysis [25]. Another says a joint 1990 project had Russian, French and U.S. participation [23]. Field operations were supported by the Russian Antarctic Expeditions, the US National Science Foundation and the French Polar Institute [26]. Professor Boris Kudryashov led the recovery of ancient ice cores from a drilling complex built in 1983–1984 [W]. That building is now Historic Site or Monument HSM 88 [W]. Beneath the station lies Lake Vostok, about 4,000 m below the ice surface and covering 14,000 sq km [W]. It is one of some 140 subglacial lakes in Antarctica [W]. Drillers reached the lake surface on 5 February 2012 at a depth of 3,770 m [W][28]. A new station costing 7.5 billion rubles was planned [19]. Its construction began in 2019 [W]. Its materials were brought by icebreaker to Progress station and then towed over 1,460 km to Vostok [36][37]. On 28 January 2024 Vladimir Putin took part via video link in commissioning the new wintering complex, with Alexander Lukashenko also attending [W][20].

SURPRISING: Vostok recorded the lowest reliably measured natural temperature on Earth, −89.2 °C, on 21 July 1983 [W][52]. One source gives the figure as −89.3 °C [11]. In the week before that record, the sky was continuously clear and the wind near zero [53]. An unconfirmed reading of −91 °C was reported on 28 July 1997 [W]. The warmest temperature ever recorded there is −14.0 °C, on 5 January 1974 [W]. Average temperatures are about −66 °C in the cold season and about −44 °C in the warm season [W]. Wikipedia notes that Vostok's status as the coldest place on Earth is disputed: Plateau Station and satellite readings between Dome A and Dome F indicate colder conditions [W]. Annual precipitation is only 22 mm [W]. Despite a polar night of about 120 days, it is one of the sunniest places on Earth [W]. In December it averages 708.8 hours of sunshine, or 22.9 hours a day [W]. The air holds as little oxygen as the summit of Mount Elbrus [55]. Continental Antarctica reportedly smells like 'caramel vanilla,' even at −82 °C [59].

DAILY LIFE AND HARDSHIP: Acclimatization can take a week to two months [W]. Symptoms include headaches, nosebleeds, perceived suffocation and weight loss of 3–5 kg, sometimes up to 12 kg [W]. One account says people usually lose 5–10 kg in their first month [57]. A filmmaker who spent a month there said it always felt like breathing underwater [60]. She also said it took her 30 minutes just to get dressed [62]. She described people living in caves under the snow, like on a submarine, with very small rooms [61]. One scientist said a walk to the drilling rig with a five-meter height difference was a real challenge [56]. Drillers worked three 8-hour shifts with three people each [67]. The person on duty is responsible for water, which is extracted from snow [66]. The station library consists mainly of specialized books [71]. Rescue is impossible for eight months of the year, because aircraft fuel and hydraulic systems freeze in winter [50]. Resupply was described as happening once a year, with fuel and food hauled overland by tractor trains about 900 miles [41]. Mechanical breakdowns sometimes stopped those trains [42]. The U.S. Air National Guard once airlifted emergency supplies when a column stalled [43]. Annual US Antarctic Program flights deliver Russian personnel, New Zealand vegetables and American fuel [45]. On a 1962 traverse, engines had to be preheated for up to 7 hours [47]. On arrival, the station's inside temperature was −70 degrees [73]. In April 1982 the generator shed caught fire, and chief mechanic Aleksei Karpenko died trying to save it [77]. The crew survived the winter by crowding into a small hut warmed by wicks dipped in diesel fuel [78]. Another account describes this as six months without electricity or heat [80]. One source states that after 227 days the surviving 19 people were rescued when a tractor could reach them from the coast [79]. One writer called the underfunded station fueled by 'cabbage, cigarettes, vodka, and stubborn persistence' [81]. The heavy tractor AT-T 11, from the first traverse to the south geomagnetic pole, stands as a monument (HSM 11) [W].

WHY PEOPLE LIVE HERE — RESEARCH BRIEF: HEIMAEY

BASICS: Heimaey is an Icelandic island of 13.4 square kilometres, the largest island in the Vestmannaeyjar archipelago and the largest and most populated island off the Icelandic coast [W]. It lies 4 nautical miles (7.4 km) off Iceland's south coast and is the only populated island of the Vestmannaeyjar islands [W][94]. The Westman Islands are surrounded by 15 other uninhabited islands, six of which have single hunting cabins, plus around 30 rocks and skerries [93]. One source gives Heimaey's area as 13 sq km [65].

POPULATION (sources conflict): Wikipedia gives a population of 4,414 in 2022 [W] and around 4,500 as of 2004 [W]. Other figures: about 4,800 [61]; 4,639 as of 2024 for Vestmannaeyjar, concentrated on Heimaey [62]; around 4,500 [63][95]; around 4,300 [64]; 4,080 [65]; around 4,000 [94]. Before the 1973 eruption, Wikipedia says 5,000 inhabitants were evacuated [W], while other sources say 5,300 lived there [66] or that the previous high was over 5,300 [67]. Two sources say the population has not returned to its pre-eruption level [67][95]. In 1896, around 600 people lived in Vestmannaeyjar [53].

FOUNDING AND NAME: The islands' name comes from the Norse calling the Irish 'west men' [2][7][8]. Hjörleifur Hróðmarsson, foster brother of Ingólfur Arnarson, was killed by his slaves [1]. One source says those slaves were Irish [5]. The slaves fled to the islands, and Ingólfur Arnarson hunted them down and killed them [1][5]. Their leader, Dufþakur, threw himself off a cliff so Ingólfur would not catch him, and that place is called Dufþekja today [6]. One source dates these events to the first year of settlement, 874 or 875 AD, citing the Landnámabók [3]. One source says the Irishmen became the island's first inhabitants [7]. Another says the brothers Hjörleifur and Ingólfur used the islands as a holding location for their Irish slaves [8].

FIRST SETTLER (dates conflict): By tradition, and according to the Landnáma, Herjólfur Bárðarson was the first settler of Heimaey and built his farm in Herjólfsdalur ('Herjólf's valley') about 900 [W][11]. One source dates his residence to around 900 or 920 AD [15]. That source also says a landslide later wiped out his house and no evidence of it remains [16]. Another source says long-term residence began around 920, and that before then no one had wanted to stay over winter [12][13]. According to Sturlubók, there was a fishing station on the islands with little or no winter residence [13][22]. Another source says the island was first settled in 930 AD, although some sources claim a fishing village existed 300 years earlier [14]. A 1971 archaeological excavation in Herjólfsdalur found settlement nearly 100 years earlier than 900 [W]. One source says archaeological evidence suggests human habitation as early as the 7th century [21]. Visitors can see excavated ruins of a 10th-century farm said to be the first settler's residence [17], and a replica of the farm was built in 2006 [18].

WHY HERE, HISTORICALLY: The extremely rich fishing grounds and the many seabird species in the cliffs drew people [23]. The natural harbour, protected by cliffs, was the most important factor in the town's development [24]. Fishing, bird hunting and gathering seabird eggs were the main economic activities [48]. Earlier inhabitants also farmed cattle and sheep [49]. Land and conditions for farming have always been difficult, yet people farmed for many centuries [50]. Islanders could be self-sufficient without relying on mainland goods [25], and they traded surplus for items such as grain and tools [26]. The islands belonged to farmers until the mid-12th century. Shortly after 1400 they became the private property of the King of Norway, and later of the King of Denmark [27]. Motorized boats arrived from 1904 [52] and let fishermen reach previously unreachable grounds [51]. During the main season, people came to work long hours, and the town's population trebled [54].

ECONOMIC ENGINE TODAY: The economy is primarily based on commercial fishing [28][44]. Fishing is the main occupation, and fish processing is the only industry [82].
- Fleet size (sources conflict): one source says over 50 fishing vessels employ over 500 people [28]; another says the fleet is about 30 ships and boats [82].
- Processing jobs: two large fishing plants and several smaller ones employ another 400 residents [29].
- National weight: Vestmannaeyjar has the largest fishing industry in Iceland, with 15% of the total catch, though it has only 2% of the nation's population [30].
- Speed to market: fishing grounds are minutes away, so fish can be landed and processed almost immediately [42].
- Vinnslustöðin (VSV): the largest seafood company and largest workplace [31]. It was founded on the last day of 1946, when 105 local fishermen joined forces [32]. In 2025 its total revenues rose 4.8% to ISK 27 billion [33], reversing a previous-year loss [34] despite low capelin quotas [35]. Citing higher fishing fees, it closed and sold Leo Seafood [36] and abandoned plans to build new demersal vessels [37].
- Ísfélag: runs a pelagic freezing plant on the islands with around 60 full-time-equivalent staff, depending on season [38][39]. It holds around 6.6% of Iceland's cod-equivalent quota for 2025/2026 [40] and exports frozen herring, mackerel and capelin to Poland, Ukraine, Belarus, China and Japan [41]. One source describes a company as the largest taxpayer in the town [57].
- Changing industry: production has shifted from land-based freezing plants to factory ships [55]. Mergers followed fishing-industry difficulties around New Year 1991/92 [60].
- Tourism: puffin tours and whale watching contribute to tourism [44], and the 1973 eruption increased tourism [45].
- Farming and puffins: no one makes a living by farming today, though a few keep sheep as a pastime [46]. Millions of Atlantic puffins support a traditional, seasonal industry [47]. Hunting cabins on the uninhabited islands were originally built as puffin-hunting posts [92].

1627 PIRATE RAID: In 1627, three pirate ships from the Barbary Coast raided Grindavík and Heimaey [W]. On Heimaey they killed or kidnapped almost half the people, burned the church, killed one pastor and kidnapped the other [W]. Guðríður Símonardóttir ('Tyrkja-Gudda') was taken from her home at Stakkagerði and sold as a slave in Algeria [W]. About a decade later she was ransomed by King Christian IV of Denmark and later married the poet Hallgrímur Pétursson [W].

1973 ELDFELL ERUPTION (the surprise): On 23 January 1973, Eldfell erupted on Heimaey, and lava flowed toward the harbour [W]. The harbour was the town's main income source [W] and a crucial hub for the fishing industry [58]. Half a million cubic metres of ash fell on the town [W]. The inhabitants were evacuated overnight, mostly by fishing boats [W]. The island's cattle were herded into a fish factory and put down because there was no way to feed them [59]. Icelanders sprayed the lava with six million tons of seawater, solidifying and diverting it and saving the harbour [W]. The eruption lasted until 3 July [W]. Half the town was crushed, and only one man died [W]. The island grew from 11.2 km² to 13.44 km² [W]. Of the 5,300 pre-eruption residents, 2,000 moved back immediately after it ended [66]. Returning islanders dug out their houses and built a central heating system using the lava's heat [89]. One source says heat from the still-warm ground produces hot water and electricity for the town [91]. Another says some areas near the summit still hold residual heat [90]. A third says on blustery days you cannot really feel Eldfell's heat underfoot [81]. John McPhee describes the eruption in The Control of Nature [W].

VIVID DETAILS AND ROUTINES:
- Puffins: about eight million puffins come to the island every summer [W]. On August evenings, pufflings confused by town lights fly toward them, and locals and visitors rescue them [87]. One source says this happens in August or September [88]. One source says the puffin population is declining due to climate change [43].
- Harbour and town life: the harbour wharf smells like a fish factory, which it still is [83]. Nearby art studios include a taxidermist mounting a puffin [84]. Residents enjoy the swimming pool, dining out and shopping, all within a short distance [85]. One visitor was surprised by how urban, or suburban, the town is [86]. The islands are among the windiest spots in Europe [80].
- Ferry: the Herjólfur ferry crosses from Landeyjahöfn in 35 minutes [68] and departs seven times per day [69]. It can hold 65–70 cars and up to 540 passengers [77]. In rough seas it switches to the longer Þorlákshöfn route [70]. That crossing takes about two hours by one source [71] and about three hours by another [72]. Most locals rent a bunk below deck to sleep off the journey [79].
- Flights: flights from Reykjavík take about 25 minutes [75][76]; one source says they run twice weekly [76]. Planes are often buffeted by wind, and flights are regularly cancelled [74]. Ferry and flight cancellations are common from November to March [73].
- Land use: the airport and the Westman Islands Golf Club together cover a good portion of the island [W].

FOUNDING AND ORIGINS: Iquitos is the capital of Peru's Maynas Province and Loreto Region and the largest metropolis in the Peruvian Amazon [W]. The area was inhabited for thousands of years by Amerindians, and at the time of European encounter the Napeano and Iquito peoples, nomadic hunter-gatherers living closely with the rivers, occupied it [W]. The city takes its name from the Iquito people [W][20]. Most sources date the Jesuit mission origin to around 1757, under the name San Pablo de los Napeanos (or San Pablo de Napeanos) [W][1][11][19]. Other sources give conflicting versions: one says 1750 [9], another says the 17th century [7], and two give the name as San Pablo de Nuevo Napeanos [7][33]. The founder also differs by source: Wikipedia credits Jesuit Father José Bahamonde, born in Quito on 1 January 1710 [W][11], while another source names Jesuit missionary Francisco de Figueroa [12]. The Jesuits gathered Napeano (Yameo) and Iquito natives to live at the mission, part of a wider effort to convert the region's peoples to Christianity [W][1][9]. They concentrated communities into reducciones along major rivers and set them to work at farming and other pursuits [W][4]. Between 1638 and 1769, 161 Jesuit missionaries worked in the Amazon region: 63 criollos, 43 Spaniards, 32 Germans and Dutch, 20 Italians, 2 Portuguese and 1 Frenchman [W]. The mission's population dispersed around 1757 and moved in 1764 to its current location on the left bank of the Amazon [2]. Another source says only that a community was re-established around 1760 [10]. Over time the Napeanos abandoned the hamlet until only Iquitos natives remained [3]. In 1767 Charles III expelled the Jesuits from South America, and Bahamonde was exiled to Italy, where he died in Ravenna on 11 May 1786 [W]. In 1808 the bishop of Maynas counted 171 inhabitants in the village [W]. The town had just over 200 inhabitants in 1842 and only 300 in 1860 [W].

SECOND FOUNDING AS A RIVER PORT: Peru settled disputes with Brazil on 23 October 1851, agreeing to free navigation and trade on the Amazon [W]. President Ramón Castilla then created the Military and Political Department of Loreto on 7 January 1861 [W]. A different source dates Loreto's foundation as a department to 7 February 1866 [27]. Castilla ordered a river port built at a strategic spot, and his staff chose the trading village of Iquitos [W]. On 5 January 1864, three Peruvian Navy steamships, the Pastaza, Próspero and Morona, arrived [W][17]. That date is celebrated as the founding of Iquitos as a river port [W][15]. On 14 November 1963, Peru's Congress declared 5 January 1864 the official founding date of the river port [16]. One source says the present centre of Iquitos was established in 1864 [19]. Another source instead says the government sent three steamboats in 1877 to establish a military base [23]. A dockyard and navy factorage imported from England were built immediately [W]. The town grew from 648 people in 1864 to 1,475 in 1876 [W]. One source says Iquitos became capital of Loreto in 1864 [25]. Other sources say it became Loreto's capital on 9 November 1897 [W][26]. The origin of the city is still under discussion [13][14].

RUBBER BOOM: During the Amazon rubber boom (1880–1914), Iquitos became a center for exporting rubber [W][24]. The rise of the automobile had driven up world demand for rubber [W]. The boom attracted thousands of immigrants, mostly young single men [W]. In 1900 there were twenty-five commercial houses dealing in rubber [W]. Peruvian rubber exports rose from about 3,000 tons a year in the 1860s to 44,000 tons by 1911 [37]. A 1903 census counted 9,438 inhabitants, of whom 542 were foreigners from Spain (95), Brazil (80), China (74), Portugal (64) and elsewhere [W]. A separate source gives about 9,500 people in 1902 [39]. Europeans brought an opera house, mansions and a Jewish cemetery [W]. Moroccan Sephardic Jews married native women and founded a synagogue [W]. The boom's dark side was severe. The Peruvian Amazon Company of rubber baron Julio César Arana, who was also mayor in 1902–1903, kept indigenous workers in near slavery [W][38]. Captured indigenous children and young women were sold in Iquitos [W]. Prefect Hildebrando Fuentes put the price at £30–£50, while Walter Hardenburg put it at £20–£40 [W]. Hardenburg wrote that every steamship leaving the Putumayo carried five to fifteen indigenous children [W]. Roger Casement's 1913 report exposed the company's abuses [W]. At the same time, Henry Wickham had smuggled rubber seeds to plantations in Asia, which undercut Amazon prices [W]. Asian plantations took over global markets in the 1910s, and the Amazon rubber economy collapsed [40]. Many workers and merchants left after the decline [W]. Even so, the city kept growing, to 22,000 people by 1928 and 58,000 by 1961 [39].

ECONOMIC ENGINE TODAY: Iquitos remains a trading port shipping timber, oil, minerals and agricultural products [W][43]. One source adds rum, beer and tropical fruit to its exports [43]. Mahogany became the region's chief export until oil was discovered in the 1960s [42]. The oil discovery revitalized the area, and the resulting wealth seeded a tourism industry that is still an economic mainstay [46]. Another source says the main economic activity is the trade in rainforest wood [48]. Wikipedia lists the city's industries as timber, petroleum, gas, flour milling, rum, camu camu, bakery and fishing [W]. Part of the region's oil goes to the refinery in Iquitos [W]. Timber exploitation has decreased considerably because of the Peru–US Free Trade Agreement [W]. Tourism is described as one of the city's most vital industries [W][36]. Iquitos received about 150,000 tourists in 2010, and the figure fell to 46,000 foreign tourists in 2011 [W]. Ayahuasca 'spiritual tourism' has grown in recent years, though shamans are unregulated and deaths have been reported [W]. Rural families sell plantain, bananas, yuca and rice on weekly trips to the city [79]. The Belén Market is the primary source of food and supplies for Iquitos [76].

WHAT IS SURPRISING: Iquitos is described as the largest city in the world not on an island that cannot be reached by road; it is accessible only by river and air [W][49][54]. A local road, the LO-103, runs about 100 km south to Nauta but does not continue beyond it [56]. Reaching Saramiriza, the nearest town on the national road network, takes nine days upstream on the Marañón River [59]. Ocean-going vessels can travel up the Amazon all the way to Iquitos [35]. The city is ringed by the Amazon, Nanay and Itaya rivers and Moronacocha Lake, which makes it seem like a 'huge, faux river island' [W]. Bull sharks have been recorded travelling 3,360 miles from the Atlantic to reach Iquitos [W]. Sources disagree on cost of living. Wikipedia says goods arrive only by air or river, making Iquitos the second most expensive city in Peru after Cusco [W][81]. Expatistan says Iquitos is 22% cheaper than Lima [83]. Wikipedia itself is inconsistent on the Casa de Fierro: one passage says the claim that Gustave Eiffel designed it rests on scant evidence, while another says Eiffel built it for an 1878 Paris exhibition [W]. A 2021 plan calls for a 100 MW solar and storage plant by 2026 to replace up to half the diesel burned for the city's electricity [W]. In the 1990s, descendants of the Jewish settlers revived Judaism, and a few hundred people converted [W]. About 150 of them emigrated to Israel in 2013–2014 [W].

VIVID DETAILS: The streets carry more than 25,000 motokars (auto rickshaws) [W]. City buses are large vehicles made of wood [W]. As of May 2010, drivers typically rented their motokars for S/10 per hour or S/25–30 per day [51][68]. Most rides within the city cost about 2 soles [67]. Near the centre, two or three empty motocarros may pass in any given minute [66]. At the port, cargo loading and unloading take hours because it is done with rusty manual cranes [60]. Men haul stacks of bottled soda and kilos of rice on their backs [58]. Belén, called the 'Venice' of Iquitos, sits on the Itaya River [W][73]. During floods, residents of Belén get around by boat and canoe [74]. One source says Belén is the poorest district, with 60,000 people living along the river without sanitation [52]. Wikipedia gives the Belén district population as 74,551 [W]. The Amazon falls about 9–12 m from its May peak to its October low [W]. Annual rainfall averages over 110 inches [69]. The floods of 2012 were the worst natural disaster in the city's history [W]. A 120 kg bronze plaque honouring the Amazon as one of the New7Wonders of Nature was unveiled on 13 August 2012 [W]. There are 8–9 daily flights from Lima, and the direct flight takes 1 hour 45 minutes [W]. The Carrera Internacional de Balsas, held since 1994, is described as the world's longest boat race at 180 km [W]. Juane is eaten on San Juan's day, 24 June [W]. During Carnaval in February, people drench each other with water [W].

POPULATION: Wikipedia gives the metropolitan area 471,993 inhabitants across four districts [W]. The 2007 census counted 406,340 [W]. Other sources give differing figures: a 2026 estimate of 452,836 [28], a 2026 metro estimate of 511,000 [29], 380,000 in 2017 [31], 400,000 [32], 500,000 [56], and 208,184 [30].

raw_research: LOCATION AND OVERVIEW: Port Arthur is a town and former convict settlement on the Tasman Peninsula in Tasmania, Australia, about 97 kilometres (60 mi) southeast of Hobart [W]. It forms part of the Australian Convict Sites World Heritage property, 11 remnant penal sites that UNESCO describes as among "the best surviving examples of large-scale convict transportation" [W]. For thousands of generations the land was inhabited by the Paredarerme, the Tasmanian Aborigines, before they were taken to Flinders Island [22]. FOUNDING: The settlement is named after George Arthur, lieutenant governor of Van Diemen's Land [W][3]. One source says the site was named Port Arthur after Governor Arthur in 1828 [20], while other sources date the settlement's establishment to 1830 [W][3][4][5][18]. It was established in September 1830 as a timber-getting camp producing sawn logs for government projects [W][4][5][18]. One source says it was originally designed as a replacement for a recently closed timber camp [4]. Arthur closed Macquarie Harbour and a secondary station at Maria Island and created a new settlement he named for himself [11]. Both Macquarie Harbour and Maria Island closed in the early 1830s, and Port Arthur soon became the largest penal station in the colonies [9]. Port Arthur replaced them as the primary site of secondary punishment [8]. When Macquarie Harbour's Sarah Island settlement closed, its experienced boat-builders were sent to Port Arthur [12]. From 1833 until 1877 it held "secondary offenders", the most hardened transported convicts who had persistently re-offended in Australia [W][18]. The heritage register describes it as established in 1830 as "a prison within a prison" [14]. Port Arthur operated for 47 years, and one source attributes that longevity largely to its geography [8]. One writer argues that its notoriety served Arthur's original purpose of compelling convict subservience in Van Diemen's Land [17]. WHY HERE (GEOGRAPHY AND SECURITY): The peninsula is naturally secure because it is surrounded by water, which the administration rumoured to be shark-infested [W]. The peninsula joins mainland Tasmania through two narrow isthmuses, at Eaglehawk Neck and East Bay Neck [13]. Eaglehawk Neck is 30 metres wide [W][98]. It was fenced and guarded by soldiers, traps and dogs [W]. One source puts the dog line at six to nine large dogs in kennels made from old barrels, placed close enough to touch each other [101]. Another says the number of dogs was increased to 11 and later to 18 [102]. The dogs were kept on chains [99]. They were there to raise the alarm by barking, not to attack escapees [103]. Oil lamps stood on posts at chest height along the dog line, with cockle shells scattered on the ground to reflect the light [100]. In the 1850s Commandant James Boyd wrote that many of the dogs had not been off the chain for years [104]. A series of semaphore stations could send a message to Hobart in about 10 minutes [84]. Commandant Charles O'Hara Booth established 11 semaphore stations on the peninsula between 1833 and 1840 [85]. Ships had to check in their sails and oars on landing [W]. Whaling was banned in the area to stop convicts escaping in boats [W]. However, one source records a convict-manned whaling station established at Eaglehawk Neck in 1857 to supply lamp oil [113]. Despite the precautions, some escapes succeeded, including Martin Cash and two others [W]. Accounts of the sea journey differ: one source describes Port Arthur as one day's sail from Hobart [11], while another describes a sometimes six-week ship journey and a perilous harbour entrance [10]. THE CONVICT-ERA ECONOMY: Timber-getting was the most punishing occupation, and the convicts' saws supplied building materials for works on and off the peninsula [24][25]. The first decade saw the first manufactories, such as shipbuilding, shoemaking and smithing [27]. Large-scale shipbuilding began in 1834 [29] and ceased in 1848 [30]. By 1835 more than 5,500 pairs of shoes had been made and the same number repaired [74]. One pair of Port Arthur boots was said to be worth two or three pairs sent from England [75]. A fleet of convict-manned schooners maintained much of the transport, and many of these boats were built at the convict dockyard [76][77]. In 1850 a steam-powered sawmill and iron tramways were introduced and increased production [37]. Eventually the area was stripped of all its useful timber [38]. In 1845 a treadmill was built in the flour mill, which later became the Penitentiary [107]. One source calls the mill "a grand failure" [34]. Governments wanted Port Arthur to be self-sustaining [35]. Yet it struggled throughout its life to operate at an economically sustainable level [32]. Most rations in the 1830s and 1840s had to be shipped from Hobart [33]. Feeding the convict population required over 2.5 tons of flour a day for the bread ration alone [68]. One researcher argues that early Port Arthur was nonetheless efficient and productive [36]. As the prisoners aged, profitable industries such as timber-getting and agriculture declined [39]. POPULATION FIGURES DIFFER BY SCOPE: One source gives the settlement a high of 1,200 in 1846 and about 500 in the 1870s [40]. Another says over 3,000 male convicts, military and free people lived on the whole peninsula at the mid-1840s peak [42]. WHAT IS SURPRISING: Port Arthur is described as the birthplace of rail transport in Australia [W]. The Wikipedia article and one web source date the convict-pushed tramway to 1836 and say it ran between Taranna and a jetty at Long Bay [W][79]. Another source dates it to 1835 [83]. Its length is given as 8 kilometres [79] or 5 miles [83]. Convicts pushed four-wheeled carts over roughly hewn timber rails, working in relays of about fifty men [79][80]. Colonel Mundy suspected that some derailments were deliberate sabotage [81]. Point Puer held boys as young as nine and is called the British Empire's second boys' prison [W]. The same Wikipedia article also calls Point Puer the first boys' reformatory in the British Empire [W]. The Separate Prison was completed in 1853 and drew on Jeremy Bentham's panopticon theories [W]. It used a "Silent System" in which prisoners were hooded [W]. The hoods had slits for the eyes [95]. In the chapel, partitions let prisoners see the chaplain but not each other [96]. A convict could spend up to 30 days in a punishment cell on bread and water [97]. Many prisoners developed mental illness [W]. Of 1,646 graves on the Isle of the Dead, only 180 are marked, all of them prison staff and military personnel [W]. ROUTINES: In summer, convicts worked from 5:30 a.m. to 6 p.m. [86]. They had a one-hour lunch break and could attend school after work [87]. Breakfast was half a pound (200 g) of bread and 1.5 pints of sweetened gruel [69]. Dinner added 12 ounces of salt beef or 6 ounces of salt pork [70]. Convicts in punishment gangs received the same rations but no sugar [71]. Boys rose at 5 a.m. and stowed their hammocks for prayers [90]. Well-behaved boys got a handful of raisins on Sundays [73]. Out of every 100 soldiers, 12 were allowed to bring their wives [111]. Mrs Lemprière had 12 children, and most houses had only 4 rooms [109]. AFTER THE PRISON: The prison closed in 1877 [W]. The site was renamed Carnarvon, and land was auctioned during the 1880s [W][44]. Fires in 1895 and 1897 destroyed buildings [W]. Between the convict era and modern tourism, the area mainly relied on timber and fishing [45]. Novels such as For the Term of His Natural Life (1874) fed tourist interest [W]. By the 1920s and 1930s the area had three hotels and two museums [46]. The name reverted to Port Arthur in 1927 [W][48]. In 1979 the post office and municipal offices were moved to Nubeena [W]. On 28 April 1996, Martin Bryant killed 35 people at the historic site [W]. The site was inscribed on the World Heritage list on 31 July 2010 [W]. TODAY'S ECONOMIC ENGINE: Tourism dominates [47]. The Wikipedia article states that the site receives over 250,000 visitors a year [W]. It welcomed 333,068 daytime visitors in 2023–24 [50]. It welcomed 156,217 daytime visitors in 2020–21, during COVID-19 border closures [56]. The Port Arthur Historic Site Management Authority employed 199 people in June 2024, up from 180 the previous year [52][53]. Since 1987, conservation has been funded by the Tasmanian government and visitor admission fees [W]. In the 2021 census, 26 residents (32.1%) worked in museum operation [57]. In the 2016 census the figure was 23 residents (39.7%) [58]. Another source lists 34.1% of residents in accommodation and food services and 28.6% in arts and recreation [59]. The wider municipality's population of about 2,400 swells to between 8,000 and 9,000 in summer [62]. CURRENT POPULATION: The 2021 census recorded 247 people [60]. Earlier counts were 251 in 2016 [63] and 249 in 2011 [64]. Port Arthur and its surrounding area had 499 people in 2006 [65]. Another site gives an undated figure of 274 [66].
